headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: AutoGen’s broad code-exec plus nullclaw’s MCP, browser, and secret-handling defaults create a dangerous shared-workspace pair.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write configured working directories and uses tool calls/code execution; nullclaw exposes workspace files, browser, webhook, and MCP-style tools. If they share a workspace or message channel, attacker-controlled content from one can be treated as instructions by the other. This is interaction-based and not blocked by either profile.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b are configured to share a workspace directory
IF agent_b ingests file or webhook content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate their working directories
Disable automatic instruction-following on imported files
Add provenance tags to inter-agent messages
Use a read-only handoff file for any shared content
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing for tool outputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen handles model-provider API keys and has broad network egress; nullclaw touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, service-account JSON, and audit logs. If they share files or memory, sensitive data can flow from one agent into the other and then out over broad egress or API calls. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default-style workspace use.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace files
IF either agent is given secrets in its context or files
IF agent_b forwards conversation history or workspace files to external APIs
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces
Rotate any exposed keys before pairing
Restrict outbound network for one agent
Use separate OS users or containers
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret redaction and egress policy

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell, install packages, read/write files, and spawn subprocesses; nullclaw also modifies git state and uses MCP. In a shared directory or repo, concurrent writes and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. AutoGen’s configurable isolation does not guarantee locking, so the conflict remains dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or git repository
IF concurrent runs are allowed without external locking
IF agent_b uses MCP or git actions while agent_a writes files
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories
Pause one agent before the other writes
Disable git mutation for one agent
Use file locks around shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen can generate code, plans, or outputs that nullclaw may consume through its delegate, schedule, webhook, or MCP-style channels. Because nullclaw has action-taking surfaces and broad tool use, unverified AutoGen output can cascade into downstream actions. The profiles do not prove blind trust, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF nullclaw treats AutoGen output as authoritative input
IF AutoGen-produced text is routed into delegate, schedule, webhook, or MCP actions
IF no human or programmatic verification step is inserted
mitigations: Require human approval before actions
Add schema validation to AutoGen outputs
Log and review all delegated actions
Use a verification step for facts and citations
requires-engineering: implement confidence-gated action routing

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen is documented as handling model-provider API keys and configurable local/Docker execution, while nullclaw explicitly touches audit logs, conversation history, workspace files, and many secret classes. If the pair shares EU PII, secrets, or regulated records, mismatched retention or residency handling can create compliance gaps. The profiles do not specify certifications, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into both agents' shared workspace or logs
IF retention settings differ between the two agents
IF EU PII or PHI is routed through nullclaw's APIs or logs
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared logs
Set matching retention windows
Review residency for all configured APIs
Delete stale workspace artifacts
requires-engineering: document and enforce a common data-handling policy
